'''''Dimorphotheca ecklonis''''', also known as '''Cape Marguerite''', '''African daisy''', '''Van Staden's River daisy''', '''Sundays River daisy''', '''white daisy bush''', '''blue-and-white daisy bush''', '''star of the veldt''', '''''Kaapse magriet''''', '''''jakkalsbos''''', '''''Vanstadensrivier madeliefie''''', or '''''Sondagsrivier madeliefie''''' is a perennial<ref>{{Cite web |title=Osteospermum ecklonis – FNA |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Osteospermum_ecklonis |access-date=2024-04-05 |website=floranorthamerica.org}}</ref> [[ornamental plant]]<ref name="SANBI">{{Cite web |title=Dimorphotheca ecklonis {{!}} PlantZAfrica|url=https://pza.sanbi.org/dimorphotheca-ecklonis|access-date=9 October 2024|website=pza.sanbi.org|language=English|url-status=live|archive-date=22 July 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240722192805/https://pza.sanbi.org/dimorphotheca-ecklonis}}</ref> that is native to [[South Africa]]. It features white ray florets and a dark blue centre and is part of the [[Asteraceae]] family. The species is named after [[Christian Friedrich Ecklon]], a Danish botanical collector who explored the flora of the Cape in the early 1800s.<ref name="SANBI" /> It is regarded as an invasive plant in parts of [[Australia]], particularly Victoria and Western Australia.<ref>Eckehart J. Jäger, Friedrich Ebel, Peter Hanelt, Gerd K. Müller (ed.): Rothmaler. Excursion flora of Germany. Volume 5: Herbaceous ornamental and useful plants. Spektrum Akademischer Verlag, Berlin Heidelberg 2008, {{ISBN|978-3-8274-0918-8}}.</ref>

==Features==
[[File:Cape Marguerite.jpg|thumb|235x235px|Closeup of a Cape Marguerite flower]]
''Dimorphotheca ecklonis'' is an [[evergreen]], [[Perennial plant|perennial]] dwarf [[shrub]] that can grow up to {{convert|1|m|sp=us}} tall.<ref name="SANBI" /><ref name="RHS">{{Cite web|title=Dimorphotheca ecklonis|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/529902/dimorphotheca-ecklonis/details|language=English|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=9 October 2024|url-status=live|archive-date=7 October 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007105739/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/529902/dimorphotheca-ecklonis/details}}</ref> The flowerheads measure up to {{convert|5|to|8|cm|sp=us}} in diameter.<ref name="SANBI" /> The leaves measure {{convert|13|to|25|by|2.5|to|10|cm|sp=us}} and are glandular fluffy, [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], [[Elliptic (leaf shape)|elliptical]], slightly [[succulent]], narrow [[obovate]], and entire or serrated. The heads are on {{convert|15|to|20|cm|sp=us}} long stems and have a diameter of {{convert|5|to|8|cm|sp=us}}. The [[bracts]] are {{convert|13|to|16|mm|sp=us}} long and glandular. The rays are white above and reddish blue below. The disc is dark blue or purple. The fruit surface is net-wrinkled.<ref>Munz, PA 1968. Suppl. Calif. Fl. 1–224. [[University of California]] Press, Berkeley.</ref>

The plant contains [[hydrocyanic acid]], making it poisonous to livestock, such as cattle, and pets, such as rabbits and rodents.<ref name="SANBI" /><ref name="RHS" />

The plant is a useful [[model organism]] for experiments because of traits such as the ability to grow quickly and all year round. It can also be used as a UV indicator because it is [[Phototropism|phototropic]] and sensitive to radiation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ávila-Avilés |first1=R. D. |last2=Torres-Gómez |first2=N. |last3=Camacho-López |first3=M. A. |last4=Vilchis-Nestor |first4=A. R. |date=2020-10-06 |title=SERS activity of hybrid nano/microstructures Ag-Fe3O4 based on Dimorphotheca ecklonis pollen grains as bio-template |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=16633 |doi=10.1038/s41598-020-73615-x  |doi-access=free|pmid=33024180 |pmc=7538885 |issn=2045-2322}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Trigona |first1=Carlo |last2=Napoli |first2=Giuseppe |last3=Pasquale |first3=Stefania |last4=Puglisi |first4=Ivana |last5=Baglieri |first5=Andrea |last6=Gueli |first6=Anna Maria |chapter=A Plant-Based Sensor for UV-A Radiation Measurements |date=May 2021 |title=2021 IEEE International Instrumentation and Measurement Technology Conference (I2MTC) |pages=1–5 |doi=10.1109/I2MTC50364.2021.9459911|isbn=978-1-7281-9539-1 }}</ref>

==Distribution==
When found naturally the plants can be seen growing at the base of cliffs or on steep hills.<ref name="SANBI" /> It is native to a small area in the [[Eastern Cape]], South Africa, around [[Uitenhage]] and [[Humansdorp]] and is found on wet grass and in [[river bed]]s at altitudes up to {{convert|300|m|sp=us}}. It prefers subtropic biomes but has been introduced into the [[Azores]], [[California]], [[Mauritius]], [[New South Wales]], [[Queensland]], [[Réunion]], [[Spain]], [[Tunisia]], [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]], and [[Western Australia]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dimorphotheca ecklonis DC. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:201468-1 |access-date=2024-03-25 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> It has become popular in Europe in places such as [[Sicily]], Italy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barone |first1=Giulio |last2=Bajona |first2=Enrico |last3=Bartolucci |first3=Fabrizio |last4=Cancellieri |first4=Laura |last5=Caruso |first5=Giuseppe |last6=Conti |first6=Fabio |last7=Domina |first7=Gianniantonio |last8=Fascetti |first8=Simonetta |last9=Franzoni |first9=Jacopo |last10=Laface |first10=Valentina L. A. |last11=Pinzani |first11=Lorenzo |last12=Rosati |first12=Leonardo |last13=Scoppola |first13=Anna |last14=Stinca |first14=Adriano |last15=Tilia |first15=Agnese |date=2023-11-20 |title=Contribution to the floristic knowledge of Lipari and Panarea Islands (Sicilia, Italy) |url=https://italianbotanist.pensoft.net/article/113415/ |journal=Italian Botanist |volume=16 |pages=59–71 |doi=10.3897/italianbotanist.16.113415 |doi-access=free |issn=2531-4033|hdl=11581/483744 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Cultivation and Propagation==
''Dimorphotheca ecklonis'' can be grown as a [[perennial]] but based on the temperature swings of the local climate it can be grown as an [[annual plant]].<ref name="UMass">{{Cite web |last=admin |date=2015-03-06 |title=Production Guidelines for Four Crops—Osteospermum, Angelonia, Calibrachoa & Ornamental Sweet Potato (Ipomoea batatas) |url=https://ag.umass.edu/greenhouse-floriculture/fact-sheets/production-guidelines-for-four-crops-osteospermum-angelonia |access-date=2024-03-25 |website=Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Growing African Daisies Will Add Bright, Vivid Color in Your Garden—Here's How |url=https://www.thespruce.com/growing-and-caring-for-african-daisies-1402912 |access-date=2024-03-25 |website=The Spruce |language=en}}</ref> The peak flowering period is in spring, although some flowers will last through summer.<ref name="SANBI" /> The plants grow fast and thrive best in full sun, in poor to moderately fertile, well-drained, sandy soil.<ref name="SANBI" /><ref name="RHS" />

It is widely used as an [[ornamental plant]] in pots and beddings.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Giovannini |first1=Annalisa |last2=Zottini |first2=Michela |last3=Morreale |first3=Giacomo |last4=Spena |first4=Angelo |last5=Allavena |first5=Andrea |date=January 1999 |title=Ornamental traits modification by Rol genes in Osteospermum ecklonis transformed with Agrobacterium tumefaciens |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s11627-999-0012-2 |journal=In Vitro Cellular & Developmental Biology – Plant |language=en |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=70–75 |doi=10.1007/s11627-999-0012-2 |bibcode=1999IVCDB..35...70G |issn=1054-5476|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In places, such as [[Australia]], where it has become invasive the white coloured flowers grow as [[groundcover]] plants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Laura |first1=Marina |last2=Consonni |first2=Roberto |last3=Locatelli |first3=Franca |last4=Fumagalli |first4=Elisabetta |last5=Allavena |first5=Andrea |last6=Coraggio |first6=Immacolata |last7=Mattana |first7=Monica |date=September 2010 |title=Metabolic response to cold and freezing of Osteospermum ecklonis overexpressing Osmyb4 |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0981942810001336 |journal=Plant Physiology and Biochemistry |language=en |volume=48 |issue=9 |pages=764–771 |doi=10.1016/j.plaphy.2010.06.003|pmid=20619667 |bibcode=2010PlPB...48..764L |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

New plants can be cultivated from seeds or cuttings.<ref name="SANBI" /><ref name="RHS" /> The plants should be propagated by seed in spring at cooler temperatures (18°C).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bass |first1=Louis N. |last2=Toy |first2=S. J. |last3=Sayers |first3=R. L. |last4=Clark |first4=D. C. |date=1967 |title=Storage of Dimorphotheca Sinuata and Osteospermum Ecklonis Seed |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23432248 |journal=Proceedings of the Association of Official Seed Analysts |volume=57 |pages=67–70 |jstor=23432248 |issn=0097-1324}}</ref><ref name="RHS" /> It is recommended that the seeds, which germinate easily, are planted {{convert|15|to|25|cm|sp=us}} from one another.<ref name="UMass" /> For propagation via cuttings, softwood cuttings should be taken in late spring and semi-ripe cuttings should be taken in late summer.<ref name="RHS" />
